stage_2_story.text_en:
When Yosef retired, he decided to transform the empty lot behind his house into a productive garden. He spent the first autumn preparing the soil — the careful cultivation of the land involved removing stones, adding compost, and testing the soil's acidity. He knew that proper groundwork would determine the success of every season to come.

As winter arrived, most of the garden lay dormant. The bare trees stood silent, and the perennial herbs he had planted — rosemary, thyme, and sage — showed no signs of life above ground. But Yosef understood that beneath the frozen surface, roots were quietly strengthening. He used this quiet period to plan his crop rotation, sketching out which beds would hold tomatoes, which would grow beans, and where the squash would climb.

When spring finally broke through, Yosef planted dozens of seeds in small trays indoors. Within ten days, the first seeds began to germinate, sending pale green shoots toward the windowsill light. He transplanted the strongest seedlings into the garden beds as soon as the last frost had passed. He also set aside a corner of the property for an orchard, planting young apple, plum, and pomegranate trees that he hoped would bear fruit within three years.

Summer was the season of rapid growth. The annual vegetables — tomatoes, cucumbers, and peppers — grew vigorously and demanded daily watering. The dense canopy of a large fig tree at the garden's edge provided welcome shade where Yosef could rest during the hottest afternoons. By July, the yield from just four tomato plants was more than his family could eat in a week.

By late August, the garden produced an astonishing abundance of fruits and vegetables. Baskets overflowed with eggplants, herbs, and ripe figs. Yosef's wife, Miriam, helped him preserve the surplus — they pickled cucumbers, dried herbs, and made jars of tomato sauce that would last through the winter months. The pantry shelves filled up with colorful jars, each one a reminder of the summer's warmth.

As autumn returned, Yosef reflected on the full cycle of his garden. He planted garlic cloves and winter onions, covered the empty beds with mulch, and pruned the young orchard trees. He felt a deep satisfaction knowing that the rhythm of the seasons — planting, growing, harvesting, and resting — would continue year after year.
